did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title attributes it to David and includes the phrase “To the tune of ‘The Doe of the Dawn.’” This phrase may refer to the melody or manner in which the psalm was performed.
The psalm opens with a direct cry to the Lord: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” This expresses a sense of being far from salvation, not necessarily a renunciation of faith.
The worshiper describes calling to the Lord day and night, yet emphasizes that he still feels no answer or relief: “But you do not answer” and “I find no rest.”
Alongside his distress, the worshiper declares that the Lord is holy and enthroned amid Israel’s praises, recalling the tradition of the ancestors who trusted in him and were delivered.

The worshiper describes himself in terms of extreme humiliation: “a worm and not a man,” “scorned by everyone,” and “despised by the people.” This highlights the contrast between the faith of the ancestors and his present condition.

The enemies are portrayed through a series of animal images: many bulls, a ravenous and roaring lion, dogs, and wild oxen. These images create a sense of danger surrounding the worshiper on every side.
The distress is also described physically: the worshiper feels poured out like water, his bones are disjointed, his heart melts, and his strength dries up.
One of the psalm’s descriptions of humiliation is the dividing of the garments and casting lots for the clothing: “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.”

In the latter half of the psalm, the language shifts from a cry for deliverance to public praise: the worshiper promises to proclaim the Lord among the congregation and fulfill his vows before those who fear him.

The psalm’s conclusion expands hope from the individual to the whole world: all the ends of the earth and the families of the nations will remember the Lord, turn to him, and bow down before him; the faith will also be passed on to generations yet unborn.
